# Can I turn the steering wheel in Honda Civic 2017 via CAN bus?

Controlling a vehicle's steering angle purely by injecting commands into the OBD-II port is a high-stakes engineering challenge, particularly when dealing with modern Electronic Power Steering (EPS) systems. Your 2017 Honda Civic LX relies on an EPS unit that actively resists driver input based on torque and position sensors. To bypass this resistance and rotate the wheel to a specific angle without driver torque, you are not simply writing to a steering angle parameter; you must effectively disable the actuator's feedback loop or trick the system into accepting the movement.

In vehicles equipped with Honda Sensing, such as the higher trims of the same model year, the architecture is often more amenable to this task because the Lane Keeping Assist System (LKAS) manages steering logic centrally. The Panda OBD dongle from comma.ai can inject frames that mimic LKAS commands, allowing the EPS to rotate the rack smoothly while the system believes an autonomous stack is controlling the vehicle. However, your LX trim lacks this hardware integration. Without Honda Sensing, the EPS control unit operates in a closed loop expecting direct driver input via torque sensors on the column.

Attempting to send raw steering angle frames to the `0x12F` (Steering Angle) or similar data IDs on the LX typically results in one of two outcomes: the wheel refuses to move because the EPS motor fights against the commanded position, or the system triggers a fault code if the discrepancy between the requested angle and the actual driver-torque input exceeds safety thresholds. The absence of a central "autonomous mode" flag means that simply broadcasting a steering command is insufficient; you are missing the permission bit that tells the EPS to yield control.

To make this work on a non-Honda Sensing vehicle, the approach shifts from sending commands to reprogramming the EPS control unit itself. This requires more than just an OBD-II dongle; it involves flashing the EPS ECU with a custom firmware or using a specialized tool like Kess3/Link to modify the calibration data. The goal is to create a scenario where the EPS ignores torque requests or enters a "steering assist" mode that allows free rotation when specific CAN IDs are present, even if those IDs are not natively supported by Honda Sensing hardware.

If you proceed with firmware modification, you must identify the specific Data Identifiers (DIDs) your XC20-based MCU expects. On many Honda platforms, there is a distinction between the steering angle report ID and the control request ID. Injecting a value to the angle report without activating the corresponding control state will likely cause the EPS motor to apply counter-torque, potentially damaging the rack or burning out the actuator if the current limits are exceeded.

The Panda OBD tool offers robust CAN frame injection capabilities, but its utility here is limited by the ECU's internal safety logic. You can verify connectivity and read live data streams easily, but writing to control registers that override physical actuators without the correct "key" in the security register or the Honda Sensing handshake will fail. The system likely checks for a specific flag indicating an autonomous system is active before permitting steering actuation via CAN bus.

Furthermore, consider the implications of sensor fusion. If you attempt to run self-driving software that outputs steering angles, your stack must also manage wheel speed data and yaw rate. The EPS unit may correlate these values to detect anomalies. If your simulated environment sends a steering command that contradicts the vehicle's dynamic state (e.g., turning sharply at high speed without corresponding lateral acceleration), the ECU may interpret this as a fault condition and disable steering assist entirely, locking the wheel in place to prevent loss of control.

Ultimately, for a 2017 Civic LX without Honda Sensing, direct CAN bus steering control via OBD-II is not natively supported without altering the underlying firmware of the EPS module. The architecture is designed to prioritize driver input over digital commands unless explicitly overridden by an integrated safety system like Honda Sensing. Any solution attempting to bypass this will require deep ECUs access and significant risk assessment regarding vehicle safety protocols.
